scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Rhumba originated in the 1930s on the East Coast of the United States, blending American big band music with Afro-Cuban rhythms like son cubano.
The 1930 recording of 'El manisero' by Don Azpiazú's Havana Casino Orchestra was pivotal, adapting Cuban son for ballroom audiences.
The rhumba craze spread internationally through Cuban artists and American big bands.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Rhumba is danced socially and competitively worldwide.
It expresses flirtation and sensual interaction between partners, with the woman’s movements signaling attraction and the man responding with desire and dominance.
It is not a sacred dance and has no noted cultural restrictions.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Rhumba music combines Afro-Cuban rhythms such as son cubano, conga, and rumba with American big band orchestration.
Instruments include saxophones, cornets, banjo, guitar, piano, violin, bass, and trap drums.
Listen for the saxophones, cornets, banjo, guitar.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 132 beats a minute.
A blend of Afro-Cuban rhythmic patterns with American big band orchestration, featuring melodic vocals and trumpet solos, producing a smooth yet rhythmically rich texture.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Don Azpiazú, who recorded 'El manisero'; Monsieur Pierre (Pierre Zurcher-Margolle), who developed International style rhumba; Antonio Machín and Remberto Lara, vocalists and soloists on key recordings; bandleaders Xavier Cugat, Jimmy Dorsey, Nathaniel Shilkret, Leo Reisman, and Enric Madriguera.

American style rhumba features a box step danced to slow-quick-quick rhythm on beats 1, 3, and 4; International style rhumba uses a quick-quick-slow pattern on beats 2, 3, and 4, inspired by Cuban bolero-son.
Rhumba descends from Cuban son and bolero-son rhythms, adapted in the US big band context.

scenes.title: Family tree

Rhumba is sibling of Mambo: Another Latin ballroom dance developed from Cuban music.
